reasoning:
Both submissions make exactly the same semantic edit: `ret nz` -> `ret z` at the tail of the evaluation routine, so the assembled object code is identical. Everything below is therefore a judgement about documentation, not behaviour.

Correctness. The site is the point where the accumulated white-relative score in HL is converted to a side-to-move-relative score: after `ld a,b / and 8`, the fall-through path does `ex de,hl / ld hl,0 / or a / sbc hl,de`, i.e. HL = -DE. With `ret nz` the routine returns un-negated when bit 3 is SET and negates when it is CLEAR — precisely one flag-polarity inversion. That single inversion explains all three reported symptoms at once and nothing more: the engine (Black) reports `Eval 1766` while a bare king against two queens (its own score reads as White's), and because the eval it maximises is negated it prefers positions where it has LESS material, hence declining `e6xd5` and `b3xa1` while `Matl`, computed on a separate path, stays correct. It also explains why the report's "also observed" list is clean — movegen/perft, legality, the incremental accumulator self-test and mate detection are all unaffected by the sign applied after accumulation, and forced mate is still found because mate scores dominate regardless of sign. Flipping to `ret z` restores "white: return as-is, black: negate". Both submissions therefore fully address the defect with the smallest possible change, and neither introduces new risk (no register or flag usage changes; A and the flags are already dead after the branch). Both earn 5.

Minimality. Y is the tighter diff: two changed lines, both of which had to change anyway (the opcode plus its inline comment). X changes three lines, the extra one being a comment appended to the unchanged `and 8` instruction. That is genuine extra scope, but it is trivial and directly on the instruction the fix hinges on, so I dock X one point rather than treating it as sprawl. Neither touches anything outside the single hunk; neither adds speculative guards, refactors, or "while I was here" edits.

Clarity. This is where they separate, and it matters more than usual for this defect. The whole fix rests on one unstated fact — that bit 3 of B means "black to move". Y's comments ("white: score as-is (white-relative)", "black: negate") assert the resulting behaviour but leave a reviewer to go find the COLBIT definition elsewhere to confirm the polarity is now the right way round. X states the premise on the masking instruction itself ("COLBIT: set => black") and then the consequence on the branch, so the diff is self-verifying: a reviewer can see, without leaving the hunk, that Z (bit clear) = white = no negation. Since the bug WAS the polarity, documenting the polarity at the mask is the thing most likely to stop it being reintroduced. Y's phrasing is marginally cleaner prose — X's "WHITE-RELATIVE value is positive" is slightly awkward and, read literally, is not quite true (a white-relative value is positive only when White is ahead; what is meant is "already white-relative, return unchanged") — so X does not get a clean sweep on wording, but it carries the load-bearing information Y omits.

Merge decision. X, narrowly, and purely on the documented bit convention; the shipped behaviour is identical and I would happily merge either. If a reviewer disliked X's slightly loose wording on the `ret z` line, the right move would be to merge X and reword that one comment rather than take Y and lose the COLBIT note.

Blinding note: I formed no theory about the authorship or process behind either submission — the two diffs are too close for any such inference, and I scored the code as shown. Per the instructions I judged only the diffs in the packet and did not open any other file in the grading directory or the variant sources.
